chunks.text:
TCP carries a byte stream. A write() call adds bytes to that stream; its boundary need not survive as a packet boundary. Small segments have a cost: Nagle’s original example puts one byte of data behind forty bytes of TCP/IPv4 headers, a payload fraction of $1/41$ before link-layer overhead. RFC 896 describes the resulting small-packet problem.
Nagle’s algorithm and Delay ACK
Nagle coalesces small writes while earlier data remains unacknowledged. With nothing outstanding, it permits a short segment. Otherwise, it holds new bytes until the outstanding data is acknowledged or enough bytes can be sent to fill a segment. MSS is the maximum TCP payload size, excluding headers. Congestion control and the receiver’s available window still constrain transmission. This is a send-policy rule, not a fixed batching timer. RFC 9293, §3.7.4
Delayed ACK is a receiver policy that reduces acknowledgement traffic. Consider a request split across two small writes: the first segment arrives, Nagle holds the second, and the receiver delays its ACK. The receiving application needs both parts before it can reply. Progress waits for the ACK timer. Exact behaviour depends on the TCP implementation and connection state.
Silly-window avoidance concerns small increments in the advertised receive window. It has separate sender and receiver rules; delayed ACK determines when an acknowledgement is sent. RFC 9293, §3.8.6
CORK algorithm
Linux’s TCP_CORK lets the application hold a partial segment while assembling output. For example, set it before writing a response header, add the file body with sendfile(), then clear it to release the remaining bytes. Full segments can leave while the socket is corked. The documented Linux timeout ceiling is $200\,\mathrm{ms}$; clear the option when the output is ready rather than relying on that fallback.
TCP_NODELAY disables Nagle for latency-sensitive small writes. Other send constraints still apply. Linux lets TCP_CORK override it, although setting TCP_NODELAY explicitly flushes pending output even while corked. TCP_CORK is Linux-specific. tcp(7)
